title: Should I buy more rental properties or pay off my existing loans?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #250 | SETTLE EXISTING LOAN OR INVEST MORE?
excerpt: A 31-year-old earning in Singapore owns three JB properties and is buying a fourth. Sean weighs gearing up against clearing debt, and suggests settling the family home first.

qa.asker: Vincent, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: Vincent is 31, works and runs a business in Singapore, and owns a semi-D in JB for his family, a condo near KSL City Mall and a unit near the RTS station, whose rents almost cover their loans. He is buying a fourth property in Perling to live in. He expects the ringgit to weaken and wants enough passive income to support his family.
qa.question: Should he keep buying properties to rent out, or focus on paying off the loans he has, and should he look at KL, Penang or Bangkok?
qa.quote: Not really about math, it's about peace of mind.
qa.answer: Both can work, depending on whether you plan to work for life and how well you sleep with debt. Since his goal is to cut his family's expenses, Sean would pay down the family home first through a flexi loan, keep the rental units leveraged, and invest only where he knows the market.

reasons.title: Earning in Singapore dollars favours leverage
reasons.body: Keep savings in Singapore dollars and use credit to own Malaysian property: as the ringgit weakens, a RM2,000 instalment feels lighter each year. If you plan to retire early instead, clearing debt makes more sense.

reasons.title: Loan interest cuts the tax on rent
reasons.body: On rent of RM3,000 a month matching the instalment, about 85% of the RM36,000 a year, roughly RM30,600, is interest that can be deducted from rental income. A fully paid unit has no such deduction, so all the rent is taxed.

reasons.title: One bad property can topple the rest
reasons.body: Rolling one property into the next works until a single bad buy, such as an abandoned project still charging RM2,000 to RM3,000 a month. Sean's own over-geared JB purchase set him back for three to four years.

reasons.title: Housing is the biggest family expense
reasons.body: Lodging takes about 30% to 35% of most families' income. Clearing the home removes that cost, and money parked in a flexi loan saves about 4% in interest while staying withdrawable.

actions: Decide whether you will keep working or want to retire early, because that decides leverage or debt-free.
Keep about six months of instalments in reserve for each property before buying the next.
Pay down your own home first, through a flexi loan you can withdraw from in an emergency.
On high-rise rentals, pay down only until the rent equals the instalment, and keep the rest of your cash free.
Invest in locations you know well rather than unfamiliar cities or countries.
qa.caveat: Without the exact loan amounts Sean keeps his answer general. In Vincent's shoes at 31 he would personally keep gearing up and delay buying his own landed home, but he stresses that risk tolerance and income differ for everyone.
